translationRepairs: After An Lushan rose in rebellion, Zhang Ke recommended him again; recalled from mourning, he was named prefect of Runan.
After An Lushan rose in rebellion, Zhang Ji recommended him again; recalled from mourning, he was named prefect of Runan.
Chinese 張垍 is Zhang Ji (垍, jì); the idiomatic English wrongly renders the given name as Ke. Independent source review confirms the correction.
When An Lushan rebelled, Zhang Ke again recommended him; he was reinstated from mourning and concurrently appointed Administrator of Runan.
When An Lushan rebelled, Zhang Ji again recommended him; he was reinstated from mourning and concurrently appointed Administrator of Runan.
Chinese 張垍 is Zhang Ji (垍, jì); the literal English wrongly renders the given name as Ke. Independent source review confirms the correction.
The rebels feared him and called him by the eye-name "Lai Chews Iron."
The rebels feared him and regarded him as "Lai Chews Iron."
目為 means regarded as or dubbed, not an eye-name; the literal rendering invents a false compound. Independent source review confirms the correction.
He was shifted to military governor of Shannan East to replace Lu Jiong, but when Prince Sihao Wang Ju reported that Jiong was still holding his ground, Zhen was returned to his former command.

He was shifted to military governor of Shannan East to replace Lu Jiong, but when Li Ju, the heir Prince of Guo, reported that Jiong was still holding his ground, he was returned to his former command.

Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. 嗣號王巨 is the Prince of Sihao, personal name Ju; Prince Sihao Wang Ju fuses the title and name unnaturally.
The emperor's wrath boiled over; an edict stripped his titles and banished him as assistant magistrate of Bozhou on a supernumerary posting.
The emperor's wrath boiled over; an edict stripped his titles and banished him as assistant magistrate of Bochuan on a supernumerary posting.
Chinese 播川 is Bochuan, not Bozhou. Independent source review confirms the correction.
The Emperor's accumulated anger burst forth; he thereupon issued an edict stripping rank and titles, demoting him to Assistant Magistrate of Bo Prefecture, with supernumerary appointment.
The Emperor's accumulated anger burst forth; he thereupon issued an edict stripping rank and titles, demoting him to Assistant Magistrate of Bochuan, with supernumerary appointment.
Literal renders 播川 as Bo Prefecture; it should be Bochuan. Independent source review confirms the correction.
At E Prefecture he was ordered to take his own life, and his property was confiscated.
On reaching Hu County, he was ordered to take his own life, and his property was confiscated.
Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. Chinese 鄠 is Hu, not E Prefecture.
When he reached E, he was granted death, and his household property was registered and confiscated.
When he reached Hu County, he was granted death, and his household property was registered and confiscated.
Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. Literal likewise mistranslates 鄠 as E.
The emperor slowly realized he had been deceived and banished Yuanzhen to Qinzhou on another charge.
The emperor slowly realized he had been deceived and banished Yuanzhen to Zhenzhou on another charge.
Chinese 溱州 is Zhenzhou, not Qinzhou. Independent source review confirms the correction.
The Emperor gradually realized Yuanzhen's slander and banished him to Qin Prefecture on another charge.
The Emperor gradually realized Yuanzhen's slander and banished him to Zhen Prefecture on another charge.
Literal mistranslates 溱州 as Qin Prefecture. Independent source review confirms the correction.
Tian Shengong—Tian Shengong was a man of Nangong in Ji Prefecture.
Tian Shengong was a man of Nangong in Ji Prefecture.
Literal needlessly doubles the personal name. Independent source review confirms the correction.
He assaulted Jing Gang at Yanzhou but failed to take the city.
He assaulted Jing Gang at Yunzhou but failed to take the city.
Chinese 鄆州 is Yunzhou; Yanzhou would be 兗州. Independent source review confirms the correction.
He attacked Jing Gang at Yan Prefecture but did not overcome him.
He attacked Jing Gang at Yun Prefecture but did not overcome him.
Literal likewise misreads 鄆州 as Yan. Independent source review confirms the correction.
When Pei Mian was slandered and the court grew suspicious, an envoy was sent to investigate; Ning's soldiers intercepted him and forcefully proclaimed Pei's innocence, and the envoy reported back.
When Pei Mian was slandered and the court grew suspicious, an envoy was sent to investigate; Ning's soldiers cut their ears to proclaim Pei's innocence, and the envoy reported back.

Chinese 剺耳 means the troops cut their ears as a pledge when declaring Pei Mian's innocence; the idiomatic version invents interception and omits the ear-cutting. Independent source review confirms the correction.
Mian was slandered and the court suspected him; an envoy was sent to inquire into the matter; Ning's troops pressed forward and plainly declared his innocence, and the envoy reported upward.
Mian was slandered and the court suspected him; an envoy was sent to inquire into the matter; Ning's troops slashed their ears and plainly declared his innocence, and the envoy reported upward.
Chinese 剺耳 is omitted; the troops cut their ears while declaring innocence, not merely pressed forward. Independent source review confirms the correction.
The barbarian host cried out to one another in alarm: "Ning is divine troops!
The barbarian host cried out to one another in alarm: "Ning is divine troops!"
The English quotation is left unclosed; the Chinese closes with ！」. Independent source review confirms the correction.

Ning heard that Yingyi had cut the rations and rewards of officers and soldiers, so that all below hated and were angry, and that he had destroyed an image of Emperor Xuanzong casting metal; he therefore told the army: "Yingyi has rebelled and rashly occupies the former emperor's old palace.

Ning heard that Yingyi had cut the rations and rewards of officers and soldiers, so that all below hated and were angry, and that he had destroyed a cast-metal image of Emperor Xuanzong; he therefore told the army: "Yingyi has rebelled and rashly occupies the former emperor's old palace.

Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. 冶金像 means a cast-metal statue of Xuanzong, not Xuanzong casting metal; the literal reverses the genitive.
His birth name was Gan; he was now granted the name Ning.
His original name was Gan; at this point the court granted him the name Ning.

Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. Chinese opens with 寧 as the named subject; the idiomatic replaces it with a pronoun and obscures who received the granted name.
At Huangcao Gorge, Wang Shouxian ambushed his vanguard with five hundred men, seized them all, entered Qianzhou, killed vice prefect Zhang Zhong, and held the city to plead for pardon.

At Huangcao Gorge, Defense Commissioner Wang Shouxian lay in ambush with five hundred men. When Zilin's vanguard arrived, it captured them all; Zilin then entered Kuizhou, killed vice prefect Zhang Zhong, and held the city while asking pardon.

Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. Idiomatic English wrongly keeps Wang Shouxian as subject of entering the prefecture and killing Zhang Zhong; the Chinese subject of 遂入夔州 is Zilin, and 夔州 is Kuizhou not Qianzhou.

Passing Huangcao Gorge, Defense Commissioner Wang Shouxian ambushed with five hundred men; when Zilin's vanguard arrived they were all captured; he then entered Qian Prefecture, killed Vice Prefect Zhang Zhong, and held the city to beg forgiveness.

Passing Huangcao Gorge, Defense Commissioner Wang Shouxian lay in ambush with five hundred men; when Zilin's vanguard arrived, it captured them all. Zilin then entered Kui Prefecture, killed Vice Prefect Zhang Zhong, and held the city while requesting punishment.
Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. Literal English renders 夔州 as Qian Prefecture; the place is Kui Prefecture (夔州).
Because his revolt had begun near loyal territory, the court made him prefect of Xiazhou and then suppression commissioner at Lizhou.
Because his original intent had bordered on loyalty, the court appointed him prefect of Xiazhou (Gorges Prefecture) and then transferred him to be suppression commissioner at Lizhou.

Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. Idiomatic Xiazhou for 峽州 collides with 夏州 earlier in the chapter; the office is Administrator of Gorges Xia (峡州).
In 796, former subordinate Han Tan, military governor of Xia-Sui-Yin, asked to clear Ning's name with the posthumous title of minister of rites, and the court allowed the family to bury him.

In 796, Han Tan, Ning's former subordinate and military governor of Xia-Sui-Yin, offered to relinquish his newly granted post of Minister of Rites in exchange for clearing Ning's name; the court then allowed Ning's family to recover and bury his body.

Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. 所加禮部尚書 is Han Tan's additional office used to petition, not clearly a posthumous title conferred on Ning.
Either way the court loses western Shu: defeat loses it outright, victory leaves it in Ning's hands.
Thus the strategic heartland of western Shu would be lost either way: defeat would lose it outright, while even victory would leave it outside the state's control.

Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. Chinese 勝亦非國家所有 does not name Ning; the idiomatic invention 'in Ning's hands' over-specifies the referent.
His son Rao Yefu, vice minister of personnel under Qianfu, was gifted in letters and eloquent debate but poor at personnel selection, and was sent out as observer of Shanzhou and Guozhou.

His son Rao, style name Yefu, in the Qianfu era was vice minister of personnel; gifted in letters and eloquent debate but poor at personnel selection, he was sent out as observer of Shanzhou and Guozhou.

Idiomatic English fuses personal name 蕘 and courtesy name 野夫 into Rao Yefu, obscuring the name/style distinction clear in the Chinese and literal English. Independent source review confirms the correction.
For losing his command he was demoted to staff officer at Duanzhou and ended as left attendant of the palace guard.
For losing his command he was demoted to military adjutant of Duanzhou and ended as Left Regular Attendant.
左散騎常侍 is Left Regular Attendant, not an attendant of the palace guard; staff officer understates 司馬. Independent source review confirms the correction.
An Zhiqing, early in Kaicheng, served as investigating censor and reported negligent suburban and ancestral rites.
An, style name Zhiqing, early in Kaicheng, served as investigating censor and reported negligent suburban and ancestral rites.
Idiomatic English fuses personal name 黯 and courtesy name 直卿 into An Zhiqing, contrary to the Chinese biography formula and the literal English. Independent source review confirms the correction.
Yan Li—Yan Li, style name Yuanming, was the younger cousin of Yan Zhen on the father's side.
Yan Li, style name Yuanming, was a younger paternal second cousin of Yan Zhen.

Independent source review confirmed the proposed correction and refined the English for accuracy and clarity. Literal English duplicates the personal name as Yan Li—Yan Li, a copy artifact not present in the Chinese.
